analysis.one_liner: Bars broadband providers from blocking or slowing lawful internet traffic or charging websites for faster delivery.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved this net neutrality bill 20-13 in 2006, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written net neutrality rules into the antitrust laws. It would have barred cable and phone companies that provide broadband from blocking, slowing, or degrading your access to any lawful website or service, from charging extra fees to escape that conduct, and from charging websites for preferential delivery. It also required providers to let people attach their own devices and to disclose service terms in plain language, while still letting them manage their networks, handle emergencies, and offer promotions.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet: the bill guaranteed that internet users could reach any lawful site, app, or service without their provider interfering or adding fees, and that websites and small online businesses could reach customers without paying broadband companies for priority. It also protected people's ability to use whatever devices they choose on their home connections.

how_it_helps.text: Broadband providers could not block, impair, discriminate against, or interfere with any person's ability to access or offer lawful content, applications, or services over the internet.
Providers could not impose an additional charge to avoid the prohibited blocking or discrimination, closing off paid 'fast lanes' for websites able to pay.
If a provider offered enhanced quality of service to a type of data, it had to offer the same enhancement to all data of that type without a surcharge, regardless of who owned the data.
Users could attach or use devices of their choice on the network, as long as those devices did not damage or materially degrade service for others.
Providers had to clearly disclose service terms and limitations in plain language.
Providers kept reasonable tools: managing their networks, prioritizing emergency communications, complying with the law, offering optional parental controls, and promotional pricing.

analysis.who_pays: Cable and telephone broadband companies: they could no longer charge content and application companies for priority delivery, could not collect fees from websites to avoid discrimination, and faced antitrust lawsuits from users and competitors if they violated the rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill constrained providers' network management: they could only take measures that were 'reasonable and nondiscriminatory' and could not discriminate between their own services and unaffiliated ones, which critics said could make it harder to address congestion.

The equal-priority requirement meant any enhanced quality of service had to be offered to all data of that type without charge, eliminating a revenue stream providers argued was needed to fund network investment.
Enforcement ran through the antitrust laws (amending the Clayton Act), which means case-by-case litigation — a slower, costlier route to compliance than direct regulator rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For internet users and small online businesses, the benefit was large and direct: a legal guarantee of access to the whole internet without interference or pay-to-play fees, with sensible carve-outs for network management and emergencies. The cost fell almost entirely on broadband companies, who would give up the ability to charge websites for priority. The main honest concern is that litigation-based antitrust enforcement is slower than direct regulation, so violations would take time and legal battles to remedy.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee passed it 20-13 and it was reported to the House in June 2006, but it sat on the Union Calendar — the waiting list for floor action — and House leaders never brought it up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2006 by Rep. Sensenbrenner with Reps. Conyers, Boucher, and Lofgren as original cosponsors, and was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The committee considered and marked up the bill on May 25, 2006 and ordered it reported (amended) by a vote of 20-13.
The committee reported the amended bill on June 29, 2006, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 303.
The reported version added provider exceptions, including offering consumer protection services, promotional pricing, and non-surcharge quality-of-service priorities.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband and cable companies came out ahead: with no law on the books, they remained free to block or degrade rival services and to charge content companies for faster delivery, and they avoided the legal exposure the bill would have created.

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and, as committee chairman, brought it to markup, where it was ordered reported 20-13.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over antitrust law
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill on May 25, 2006 and reported it amended by a 20-13 vote on June 29, 2006.

for.name: John Conyers Jr., Rick Boucher, and Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced; Conyers was the committee's top Democrat.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote; after it was placed on the Union Calendar on June 29, 2006, no floor action was taken before the Congress ended.

against.name: Broadband and cable industry
against.role: Cable and telephone companies providing internet service
against.what_they_did: Opposed net neutrality legislation during the 2006 debate, arguing paid prioritization and network management freedom were needed to fund network investment.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican chairman sponsored the bill and his committee approved it 20-13, with the five known cosponsors all Democrats — but because it never reached a floor vote, the full chamber never took sides, and opposition surfaced mainly as an absence of floor action.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from charging websites for faster delivery, collecting fees to avoid discrimination, or interfering with users' access to lawful services. Its core business interest — charging for prioritized access and favoring its own content — ran directly against open access for internet users.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and service companies
industries.note: The bill guaranteed these companies nondiscriminatory access to every broadband subscriber without paying providers for fast lanes, and gave them the same equal-treatment right as the provider's own services.
